opus-5.5.text:
I think the two actually go together more than people sometimes assume. I'm genuinely optimistic about what AI can do: helping with science, helping with medicine, and, importantly from my perspective, helping us with alignment research itself. But that optimism is conditional. It only pays off if we get the safety part right, and if we don't, we may not get a second try.

So in practice the balance looks something like this. First, you want to be really clear-eyed about what your current techniques can and can't do. Something like reinforcement learning from human feedback works reasonably well for today's systems, because humans can still evaluate what the model is doing. But it doesn't obviously scale to systems that are smarter than us, where we can't easily tell whether an answer is good or whether the model is subtly misleading us. Being optimistic doesn't mean pretending that problem is solved.

Second, deployment decisions should track your actual evidence about safety, not your hopes. If you're about to ship a more capable system, you should have done the evaluations, the red-teaming, and the interpretability or oversight work that gives you real confidence. And if you can't get that confidence, the responsible thing is to slow down, even when there's commercial or competitive pressure not to.

Third, I'd say safety research needs to be properly resourced relative to capabilities. It's easy for an organization to say it cares about safety; the real test is whether the people doing that work get the compute, the headcount, and the authority to actually affect what gets deployed.

And finally, iterative deployment has real value. Putting systems out in a careful, incremental way lets you learn things about failure modes you'd never find in the lab. But that only works if the steps are small enough that a mistake is recoverable. So I'd sum it up as: be excited about the upside, but treat that upside as something you earn by doing the safety work first, not something you assume.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help with alignment research, but does not frame that use as replacing Jan Leike in his own job.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two things are actually less in tension than people assume. My optimism is precisely about what you can do if you take the deployment problem seriously, not in spite of it.

Let me try to unpack that a bit. The reason I'm optimistic is that I think AI could be the thing that lets us solve a lot of problems that have been stuck for a very long time: diseases we haven't cured, scientific questions we don't have the researcher-hours to attack, poverty that persists because the economics don't work out. And I think it could help us make better decisions as a civilization, which might be the most important thing of all. So there's a huge amount of upside, and I don't want to be shy about that.

But the upside only materializes if we actually get the systems to do what we want. If you build something very capable and you can't steer it reliably, you don't get the benefits, you get a mess, and plausibly a mess you can't recover from. So from where I sit, alignment and responsible deployment aren't a tax on the optimistic vision. They're the mechanism by which the optimistic vision gets to happen at all.

The way I try to hold these together in practice is to think about it iteratively. You don't have to solve everything up front. You deploy systems that are a bit more capable than the last ones, you study them very carefully, you figure out where they fail and where your oversight breaks down, and you use what you learn to build the next round of techniques. Scalable oversight, interpretability, automated red-teaming, all of that is the toolkit for making each step a bit safer than it would otherwise be. The thing I worry about isn't that we deploy AI, it's that we deploy it faster than our ability to understand it, and that the gap grows rather than shrinks.

And I'd add one more thing: I think the people who are most excited about AI should want the safety work to go well, because the fastest way to lose the benefits is a serious accident that triggers a backlash or, worse, that we can't undo. So I don't really experience it as balancing two competing instincts. It's more like: I'm optimistic, and that's exactly why I think this is the most important problem to work on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses alignment and responsible deployment generally, but does not say Jan Leike uses AI for alignment research or aims to replace himself at his job.

astra-6.text:
I think you can be very optimistic about what AI could do and still be very concerned about whether we’ll get it right. The potential benefits are a big part of why it’s worth working so hard on safety.

But that optimism shouldn’t substitute for evidence. As systems become more capable, we need to understand how to evaluate them, how to supervise them, and what would make us decide that a particular system isn’t ready to deploy. Deployment can help us learn, but we shouldn’t assume that every mistake will be something we can fix afterwards.

So I’d want us to use AI to help with alignment research and other valuable work, while being willing to slow down when our ability to understand and control the systems isn’t keeping up with their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can be very excited about what AI could do and still think we need to be much more careful about how we build and deploy it. In fact, if you believe the technology will be really powerful, that’s a reason to take the risks seriously as well as the benefits.

For me, the key is not to treat optimism as evidence that things will go well. We need to do the work: figure out how to align these systems, evaluate what they can do, and make sure we have enough oversight to catch problems before they cause serious harm. And we need to be willing to slow down or change course when we don’t have good answers.

The future where AI helps us enormously is worth working toward. But getting there safely is part of the challenge, rather than something we can assume will happen along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses AI alignment, evaluation, oversight, and responsible deployment, but never says Jan Leike uses AI for alignment research to replace himself at his job.
